prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states that founded the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a discovery in which a prediction from electronic-structure reasoning was confirmed by a decisive experiment. Bistritzer and MacDonald showed in 2011 that interlayer tunnelling in a continuum model flattens the bands at a magic angle, and Jarillo-Herrero's group found correlated insulators and gate-tunable superconductivity in 2018. The twist angle became a continuous control parameter for band structure and strong correlations, which is new in condensed-matter physics. It has since been reproduced by many independent groups with transport, scanning-probe and optical methods, and it has spread to other moire platforms and to fractional Chern insulators. The physical idea is clear and the continuum-model picture is now standard. A theory-plus-experiment trio is a natural prize structure with a clean citation. I also hold that discoveries which change what we expect from band theory deserve priority, and graphene already showed how an experimental discovery can overturn assumptions about what is stable.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Eva Andrei's early STM and transport evidence for van Hove singularities and flat-band physics in twisted graphene is a real claim, and a three-person limit forces a choice that is hard to defend on priority grounds alone. The field is also only eight years old, and the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still contested, so the citation must rest on the flat bands and the correlated phases, not on a settled microscopic theory. Finally, optical lattice clocks (B001) have the broadest opening support, and I rated them fifth partly because precision metrology is outside my own expertise; I should not let my own field bias push a fast-moving area ahead of a more mature one without testing the argument.

responses.point: Pearce ranked B013 second but proposed MacDonald, Andrei and Jarillo-Herrero, arguing that Andrei's STM evidence for van Hove singularities and flat bands is an important complementary observation and that excluding Bistritzer is a credit tension.
responses.response: I take the Andrei claim seriously, but I come out differently. The prize rationale is the prediction of the magic-angle flat bands and the discovery of the correlated and superconducting phases that followed from them. Bistritzer and MacDonald carry the first and Jarillo-Herrero the second. Andrei's STM work reported twist-dependent van Hove singularities and Fermi-velocity renormalisation. That is real physics, but it came before the magic-angle prediction and did not discover the correlated or superconducting states. Dropping Bistritzer to make room would remove the person who co-wrote the continuum model, and I do not think the committee can credit MacDonald alone for that paper. I would make the exclusion of Andrei explicit in our deliberations and not silently drop her. Your point shows that this is the most contestable choice in the configuration.

responses.point: Johansson ranked B013 fifth and called it possibly slightly early, since the field is about eight years old and the superconducting pairing mechanism is still debated, while placing circuit QED first and the lattice clocks second.
responses.response: I accept that the pairing mechanism is unsettled, and I would not write a citation that mentions it. I do not accept that this makes the prize premature. Our test is whether the discovery is secure and independently reproduced, not whether every follow-up question is closed. The correlated insulators and superconducting domes have been reproduced across devices, laboratories and several moire platforms. The flat-band prediction was made in 2011 and confirmed by the experiments, so the prediction-to-confirmation chain is already long. On your first choice, circuit QED, I would point to the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits. That is a near-term overlap that twisted bilayer graphene does not have. I do agree that your lattice clock ranking is an alternative I should keep open.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked optical lattice clocks first for the magic-wavelength idea, the 1e-18 accuracy and the link to redefining the second, while asking whether the committee sees the work as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes and whether other early lattice-clock groups are adequately credited.
responses.response: The case for Katori and Ye is strong, and I moved nothing against it on scientific grounds. Two names fit a two-person credit, the clocks are reproduced in several national laboratories, and the redefinition of the second is on the table. My hesitation is the one you list. Frequency-comb metrology was honoured in 2005 and single-ion clocks in 2012, so a lattice-clock prize would be the third precision-frequency prize in twenty-five years, and Lemonde's and other groups' roles are unresolved. I would not call that disqualifying. It is a reason I rank twisted bilayer graphene first, where the conceptual break is sharper, and keep B001 as a leading alternative. I also concede that metrology is outside my expertise, so I would give your and Lindroth's judgment on the originality of the lattice scheme considerable weight.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked B013 first and B008 third, and said that the infinite-dimension limit and the impurity-problem mapping make dynamical mean-field theory a decisive but credit-complicated advance, with Metzner and Muller-Hartmann affecting the allocation.
responses.response: I agree that the credit problem in B008 is serious and that Metzner is missing from the supplied names. I ranked it third because I use the method and know how well it works for real materials. I also know that results for real materials depend on double-counting and impurity-solver choices. For these reasons I would not push B008 forward this round, and I am not including it among my alternatives. I would like to hear whether you see a way around the missing Metzner credit within three of the supplied names.

uncertainties: Whether Andrei should displace Bistritzer or Jarillo-Herrero. Priority for the early STM observations versus the magic-angle prediction is a judgment I cannot settle from the supplied credit alone.
Whether the committee will see a prize for a field starting in 2018 as timely or as early, given the open pairing mechanism.
Whether the 2016 topological-phases prize and the 2010 graphene prize make colleagues treat a condensed-matter prize on twisted graphene as too close to recent recognition.
How much weight to give the broad opening support for B001 against my own lower ranking, which I attribute partly to unfamiliarity with precision metrology.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the preferred configuration. My documented ties are to Uppsala, Los Alamos and my doctoral supervisor, none of which is connected to Bistritzer, MacDonald or Jarillo-Herrero. I do use dynamical mean-field theory, so I would flag a possible perspective bias if B008 were seriously considered, and I would consider recusing myself from a decision on it.
